power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Forty-two adults were recruited through the university's experiment-participation platform and tested in the Health Psychology laboratory at KU Leuven. Three participants with cold-related obstructed breathing or excessive movement were excluded before statistical analysis. The final sample comprised 39 participants, aged 18-21 years (M = 18.59, SD = 0.88). 34 reported female and five male sex assigned at birth. All completed the four conditions. Six participants reported formal musical training (M = 6.0, SD = 2.37). Among the 39 participants, 15 performed physical exercise or sports 1-2 times per week, 13 exercised 3-4 times per week, four exercised at least five times per week, six never exercised, and one preferred not to say. The recruitment target of 40 allowed for 10% attrition and was based on a G*Power analysis for a four-condition within-participant design, assuming Cohen's f = .25, α = .05, and 80% power, informed by Van Diest et al. (2014). Eligibility required age 18-35 years and comprehension of written and spoken English. Exclusion criteria were recent psychotropic-medication use; cardiac or respiratory disorders, hearing impairment, or psychiatric disorders within the preceding two years; pregnancy; and breathing-exercise or mindfulness practice at least twice weekly during the preceding month. Participants avoided strenuous exercise and alcohol for at least 12 h before testing. They provided written informed consent and received course credits. The KU Leuven ethics committee approved the study (G-2025-10319).

table.title: Adaptive and Immersive Respiration Sonification to Induce Relaxation
table.research_questions:
Primary confirmatory hypotheses
H1. Respiration rate (RR).
Auditory stimulation will modulate respiration rate relative to Static. Specifically:
•	RR will be higher in Speeding than Static.
•	RR will be lower in Slowing than Static.
•	RR will be lowest in Adaptive Delayed, reflecting entrainment toward slower breathing.
Predicted ordering: Speeding > Static > Slowing ≥ Adaptive.

H2. Auditory–respiratory phase locking (MPC).
Auditory–respiratory MPC during stimulation will be stronger in conditions that promote entrainment. Specifically:
•	MPC will be highest in Adaptive Delayed.
•	MPC will be higher in Slowing than Speeding.
Static is non-oscillatory and therefore does not have a defined stimulus phase; MPC is not computed for Static.
Predicted ordering (oscillatory conditions): Adaptive ≥ Slowing > Speeding.

H3. Respiration-synchronous cardiac modulation (RSA).
RSA will increase in conditions that induce slower breathing. Specifically:
•	RSA will be higher in Slowing and Adaptive than Static.
•	RSA will be lower in Speeding than Static.
Predicted ordering: Speeding < Static < Slowing ≤ Adaptive.

H4. Subjective relaxation (SRSI3-qt).
Relaxation will be higher in Slowing and Adaptive than Static and lowest in Speeding.
Predicted ordering: Slowing ≈ Adaptive > Static > Speeding.

________________________________________

Secondary hypotheses and exploratory analyses
H5. Cardio-respiratory coupling.
Cardio-respiratory phase synchrony will be higher in Slowing and Adaptive than in Speeding (reflecting stronger coupling under slower respiration).

H6. End-tidal CO₂ (ETCO₂).
ETCO₂ will decrease in Speeding (relative hyperventilation) and increase in Slowing and Adaptive; Static will show minimal change.
Predicted ordering: Speeding < Static < Slowing ≤ Adaptive.

H7. EMG (upper trapezius).
EMG will be higher in Speeding than Static and lower in Slowing/Adaptive than Static.
Predicted ordering: Speeding > Static > Slowing ≥ Adaptive.

H8. Hyperventilation symptoms (Nijmegen).
Nijmegen scores will show the inverse pattern of relaxation, with higher scores in Speeding than Static and lower scores in Slowing/Adaptive than Static.

Note on fixed-band HRV (HF/LF).
We will compute HF-HRV (0.15–0.40 Hz) and LF-HRV (0.04–0.15 Hz) as secondary autonomic indices. However, because respiration frequency may slow below 0.15 Hz in Slowing/Adaptive conditions, respiration-related variability may shift from HF to LF. Therefore, we do not treat “HF-HRV increases” as a strict confirmatory prediction independent of achieved respiration rate; fixed-band HRV results will be interpreted relative to the observed breathing frequency.

RMSSD (secondary vagal index).
In addition to RSA, we will compute RMSSD from artifact-corrected RR intervals as a conventional time-domain parasympathetic HRV measure. RMSSD will be analyzed using the same difference-score and mixed-effects models as other cardiac outcomes. This serves as a secondary/sensitivity analysis for robustness and comparability with HRV literature.

Phase difference at stimulus onset.
For oscillatory conditions, we will examine whether the auditory–respiratory phase offset at stimulus onset predicts subsequent respiratory variability during stimulation (e.g., variability of breath duration). Phase offset will be modeled using sine and cosine components. These analyses are exploratory.

Order effects.
We will test for potential order effects by including trial number as a covariate in primary models and examining Condition × TrialNumber interactions. These analyses are exploratory and intended to assess possible habituation or carryover effects.

table.study_design_overview:
The study investigates how auditory stimuli resembling human breathing sounds influence physiological relaxation and respiratory entrainment. The auditory stimulus is designed to mimic natural breathing patterns through amplitude-modulated pink noise filtered to evoke an “ocean-like” sound. The sound is played at a comfortable listening level individually adjusted by each participant prior to the start of the experiment.

Each participant completes four experimental conditions presented in counterbalanced order:
- Static: A steady, filtered sound with no rhythmic modulation.
- Linear Decay: An oscillatory sound that gradually slows down (linearly decreasing tempo) across a 4-minute stimulation period.
- Linear Increase: An oscillatory sound that gradually accelerates down (linearly increases tempo) across a 4-minute stimulation period.
- Adaptive Phase-Delay: An oscillatory sound that adapts in real time to the participant’s ongoing breathing rhythm and phase but with a slight temporal delay, designed to gently guide respiration toward slower rates through entrainment.

At the start of each condition, the stimulus tempo is initialized to the participant’s own mean breathing rate, computed from a 30 second baseline period of spontaneous breathing recorded immediately before the auditory stimulus period.

Each trial lasts 8 minutes in total, consisting of a 4-minute silent baseline phase followed by 4 minutes of auditory stimulation.

Participants are instructed to sit comfortably and remain still while listening to the sounds. No explicit instructions are given regarding breathing rate, attentional focus, or eye closure. After each condition, participants will complete a brief questionnaire about their subjective experience, including attention, relaxation, and whether their eyes were open or closed during the trial. Throughout the session, non-invasive physiological signals will be recorded continuously (respiration, electrocardiogram, trapezium muscle EMG, and end-tidal CO₂) to assess physiological changes associated with the different sound conditions.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants will be sampled from the KU Leuven student and staff population and the wider Leuven community (Belgium). Recruitment will occur via (i) the KU Leuven Experimental Management System, (ii) flyers posted on KU Leuven campuses, and (iii) online participant recruitment posts (e.g., local Facebook groups). Recruitment and testing will be conducted by a trained master’s student in the Health Psychology Laboratory at KU Leuven (Leuven, Belgium).

Interested individuals will first complete an online screening/background questionnaire hosted on the secure KU Leuven Microsoft Forms platform. This screening will confirm eligibility and collect basic demographics and relevant background variables (e.g., age, sex, health screening items, mindfulness/breathing practice frequency). Eligible individuals will receive a coded participant ID and a link to schedule a laboratory appointment. Informed consent will be obtained in person at the start of the lab session, after participants have received and read the GDPR information letter and had an opportunity to ask questions.

Inclusion criteria are: (1) age ≥ 18 years, and (2) sufficient proficiency in written and spoken English to understand instructions and questionnaires. Exclusion criteria are: (1) recent use of psychotropic medication, (2) self-reported or diagnosed cardiac or respiratory disorders, (3) self-reported or diagnosed hearing impairment, (4) self-reported or diagnosed psychiatric disorder within the past 2 years, (5) regular breathing exercises or mindfulness practice (≥2 times/week in the past month), and (6) pregnancy. To reduce acute physiological confounds, participants will be instructed to refrain from strenuous exercise and alcohol for at least 12 hours prior to testing.

The target sample size is N = 40 usable datasets. Data will be collected in a single in-lab session per participant (approximately 90 minutes, including sensor setup, baseline, four experimental conditions, questionnaires, and debrief). Data collection will continue until N = 40 usable datasets are obtained. Based on typical recruitment and laboratory throughput, the expected duration of data collection is approximately 6–10 weeks, allowing for no-shows and rescheduling.

This study primarily involves new data collection. Physiological recordings (respiration, ECG, EMG, ETCO₂) and questionnaire responses will be acquired prospectively during the lab session. Raw physiological data will be stored immediately under the participant’s coded ID on secure institutional storage. No data preparation prior to analysis will be performed. No inferential analyses will be conducted until data collection has ended.
table.sample_size:
Unit of analysis.
The primary unit of analysis is the participant in a fully within-subject repeated-measures design.

Planned sample size (participant level).
We aim to obtain N = 40 usable participants. Each participant completes all four auditory conditions (Static, Linear Increase, Linear Decay, Adaptive Delayed). Therefore, the participant-level sample size is expected to be identical across conditions (n = 40 per condition) for all condition-level analyses.

Nested data structure.
The data have a hierarchical structure:
- Level 3: Participant (N = 40)
- Level 2: Condition (4 per participant)
- Level 1: Time bins within condition
Each condition consists of:
- 4 minutes baseline
- 4 minutes stimulation
Physiological time series will be segmented into 30-second bins, yielding:
- 8 bins per baseline segment
- 8 bins per stimulation segment
- 16 bins per condition
- 64 bins per participant (4 conditions × 16 bins)
Thus, bin-level analyses will involve repeated observations nested within participant × condition.

Segment-level and difference-score analyses.
For primary analyses, physiological variables (e.g., respiration rate, RSA, ETCO₂, EMG RMS, phase coherence metrics) will be summarized at one of two levels:
- Bin-level analyses using linear mixed-effects models with participant as a random effect and time (bin) modeled as a continuous predictor.
- Segment-level summaries, computed as the mean across bins within baseline and stimulation segments.
In addition, for several outcomes we will compute difference scores within condition: Difference Score = Stimulation Mean − Baseline Mean. These difference scores yield one observation per participant per condition (n = 40 per condition) and will be used in confirmatory analyses testing the effect of auditory condition on physiological change.

Unequal sample sizes and missing data.
The target N = 40 refers to usable datasets after exclusions (e.g., major signal loss, protocol violations). Recruitment will continue until 40 complete and analyzable participant datasets are obtained. Missing bins due to transient artifacts will be handled within mixed-effects models; participants with unusable full-condition recordings will be excluded prior to analysis.
table.stopping_rule:
Starting rule.
Pilot testing will conclude once (1) all equipment and signal acquisition pipelines (respiration, ECG, EMG, ETCO₂, audio adaptation) operate reliably for a full session without technical failure, and (2) the experimental timing, binning (30-second windows), and preprocessing scripts are finalized. No pilot data will be included in the confirmatory analyses. Formal data collection will begin only after the protocol, preprocessing steps, and analysis plan are fixed.

Stopping rule.
Data collection will terminate when N = 40 usable participant datasets have been obtained (i.e., complete sessions with analyzable physiological data across all four conditions), or when the predefined data-collection window ends, whichever occurs first. Recruitment will continue until 40 complete and valid datasets are achieved.
table.manipulated_variables:
The study includes one experimentally manipulated variable: Auditory Stimulation Condition (within-subject factor; 4 levels):
1. Static – Continuous filtered pink noise without rhythmic modulation.
2. Linear Increase – Breath-like amplitude-modulated pink noise with linearly increasing tempo over the 4-minute stimulation period.
3. Linear Decay – Breath-like amplitude-modulated pink noise with linearly decreasing tempo over the 4-minute stimulation period.
4. Adaptive Delayed – Breath-like amplitude-modulated pink noise that adapts in real time to the participant’s respiration rhythm and phase, with a slight phase delay designed to promote gradual slowing through entrainment.
Each participant completes all four conditions. Condition order is counterbalanced across participants.
No additional variables are experimentally manipulated.

table.indices:
1. Respiration Rate (RR)
Computed breath-by-breath as: RR = 60 / breath_duration_seconds where breath_duration_seconds = inhalation_time + exhalation_time.
RR will be averaged within each 30-second bin and then averaged across bins within baseline and stimulation segments when required.

2. Inspiratory–Expiratory Ratio (IER)
IER = inhalation_time / exhalation_time computed per breath and aggregated per bin or segment.

3. Breath Variability
Coefficient of Variation (CV): CV = standard_deviation(breath_duration) / mean(breath_duration). Lag-1 autocorrelation: AR1 = autocorrelation of breath_duration at lag 1. Both computed within segment.

4. Within-Condition Difference Scores
For outcomes analyzed as change scores: Delta_Y = mean(Y_stimulation) - mean(Y_baseline). Means are computed across 30-second bins within each segment. This yields one difference score per participant per condition.

5. Auditory–Respiratory Synchrony (Mean Phase Coherence; MPC)
Respiratory phase and stimulus phase will be extracted using the Hilbert transform. MPC = absolute_value( (1/N) * sum over k of exp( i * (phi_res_k - phi_aud_k) ) ). Values range from 0 (no synchronization) to 1 (perfect phase locking). Computed per 30-second bin and averaged per segment.

6. Cardio-Respiratory Synchrony
Computed using the same MPC formula applied to cardiac phase and respiratory phase: MPC_cardioresp = absolute_value( (1/N) * sum over k of exp( i * (phi_card_k - phi_res_k) ) ). Additionally, magnitude-squared coherence may be computed using Welch spectral estimation.

7. RSA (Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia)
Time-domain method: RSA_per_breath = IBI_max_within_breath - IBI_min_within_breath. Segment RSA = mean(RSA_per_breath across breaths)
Frequency-domain method: HF_power = spectral power of RR interval series in 0.15–0.40 Hz band (using detrending, interpolation, and Welch PSD). HF power may be log-transformed if skewed.

8. HRV Spectral Power
RR intervals will be: 
- Detrended
- Interpolated to uniform sampling
- Power spectral density estimated via Welch method
Indices:
- LF_power = spectral power in 0.04–0.15 Hz band
- HF_power = spectral power in 0.15–0.40 Hz band
Log transformation applied if distribution is skewed.

9. ETCO2
Breath-by-breath ETCO2 = maximum CO2 value during expiration plateau (mmHg).
Segment ETCO2 = mean(ETCO2 across valid breaths within segment).
Breaths without a reliable expiration plateau will be excluded.

10. EMG RMS
RMS = sqrt( mean( signal^2 within 0.5-second sliding window ) ).
Segment EMG = mean(RMS across segment).
Normalized EMG: EMG_normalized = RMS_segment / RMS_MVC where RMS_MVC is maximal voluntary contraction during calibration.

All indices will be computed identically across participants and conditions. Continuous predictors in statistical models will be mean-centered.
table.statistical_tests:
All dependent variables (DVs) will be analyzed separately. Analyses will be conducted using linear mixed-effects models (LMMs). Statistical significance will be evaluated using Satterthwaite approximation for denominator degrees of freedom. Alpha = .05 (two-tailed). Unless otherwise stated, the primary confirmatory models will use treatment (dummy) coding with the Static condition as the reference level. Sum-contrast coding will be used as a sensitivity analysis to verify robustness of conclusions to coding scheme.

1. Primary Confirmatory Analysis: Condition Effects on Change Scores
For physiological and self-report outcomes, we will compute within-condition change scores:
Delta_DV = mean(DV_stimulation) − mean(DV_baseline)
Means are computed across 30-second bins within each segment.
Model 1 (Primary Model)
Delta_DV ~ Condition + (1 | Participant)
•	Condition levels: Static (reference), Speeding, Slowing, Adaptive Delayed.
•	Each coefficient represents the difference between that condition and Static.
Planned Comparisons
1.	Speeding vs Static
2.	Slowing vs Static
3.	Adaptive vs Static
4.	Adaptive vs Slowing
5.     Adaptive vs Speeding
6.     Speeding vs Slowing
Holm correction will be applied within each DV.
An omnibus likelihood-ratio test comparing Model 1 to a model without Condition will also be reported.
________________________________________
2. Sensitivity Analysis: Sum Coding
As a robustness check, we will refit the primary model using sum-contrast coding:
Delta_DV ~ Condition + (1 | Participant)
Under sum coding, the Condition main effect tests deviation from the grand mean. Conclusions will be considered robust if pattern and significance are consistent across coding schemes.
________________________________________
3. Growth-Curve Analysis (Time-Resolved Dynamics)
To examine temporal dynamics during stimulation, 30-second bins will be analyzed.
Time will be treated as continuous and centered (0–7 bins). A quadratic term will be included.
Time2 = Time^2 (computed after centering).
Model 2 (Stimulation-Only Growth Model)
DV_bin ~ Condition * Time + Condition * Time2
+ (1 | Participant)
+ (1 | Participant:Condition)
Primary tests:
•	Condition × Time
•	Condition × Time2
These test whether linear and quadratic trends differ across conditions.
If convergence permits, we will include a random slope for Time within Participant:
DV_bin ~ Condition * Time + Condition * Time2
+ (Time | Participant)
+ (1 | Participant:Condition)
If the maximal model yields singular fit or fails to converge, random slopes will be removed.
________________________________________
4. Baseline vs Stimulation Slope Comparison
To directly compare temporal trends between baseline and stimulation segments, we will define:
Segment = Baseline vs Stimulation
TimeWithinSegment = 0–7 within each segment
Time2WithinSegment = squared centered time
Model 3 (Segment-Slope Model)
DV_bin ~ Condition * Segment * TimeWithinSegment
+ Condition * Segment * Time2WithinSegment
+ (1 | Participant)
Primary tests:
•	Segment × TimeWithinSegment
•	Segment × Time2WithinSegment
•	Condition × Segment × TimeWithinSegment
•	Condition × Segment × Time2WithinSegment
These test whether stimulation changes slope relative to baseline and whether this change differs by condition.
________________________________________
5. Baseline-as-Covariate Model (Optional Sensitivity Model)
As a sensitivity analysis, we will test an ANCOVA-style model:
DV_stimulation_mean ~ Condition + DV_baseline_mean + (1 | Participant)
This model adjusts stimulation means for baseline differences. If baseline covariate is non-significant and conclusions match Model 1, Model 1 remains primary.
________________________________________
6. Correlation Matrix (Exploratory)
We will compute a correlation matrix between:
•	Trait measures (MAIA-2, MISS, ITQ, musical training, baseline RR, etc.)
•	Primary change scores (Delta_RR, Delta_RSA/HF-HRV, Delta_MPC, Delta_ETCO2, Delta_EMG, Delta_SRSI)
Pearson correlations will be used (Spearman if distributions are non-normal).
False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction will be applied across correlations.
These analyses are exploratory.
________________________________________
7. Moderation Analyses (Limited, Preregistered)
To test whether individual differences moderate condition effects, we will conduct moderation models for a limited set of moderators:
•	Interoceptive awareness (MAIA-2 total)
•	Susceptibility (MISS)
•	Immersive tendencies (ITQ)
•	Baseline respiration rate
Moderators will be mean-centered.
Model 4 (Moderation Model)
Delta_DV ~ Condition * Moderator + (1 | Participant)
Significant interactions will be followed by simple slopes analysis at:
•	−1 SD
•	Mean
•	+1 SD
Holm correction applied across moderation tests within each DV.
_____________________________________________________________________
8. Repeated-Measures ANOVA (Complementary Analysis)
In addition to linear mixed-effects models, we will conduct repeated-measures ANOVA on participant-level change scores (Delta_DV) and stimulation-segment means to compute standardized effect sizes and facilitate comparison with previous literature. Model specification: Delta_DV ~ Condition (within-subject factor with 4 levels)
•	Sphericity will be tested using Mauchly’s test.
•	If violated, Greenhouse–Geisser correction will be applied.
•	Partial eta squared (eta_p^2) will be reported as effect size.
Planned contrasts (as specified above) will be tested within the ANOVA framework using Holm correction. ANOVA results will be interpreted as complementary to the primary mixed-effects analyses. Primary confirmatory inference will remain based on the linear mixed-effects models.
________________________________________
8. Assumption Checks and Decision Criteria
•	HRV LF and HF power will be log-transformed if skewed.
•	Residual vs fitted and Q–Q plots will be inspected.
•	If heteroscedasticity persists, robust standard errors will be reported as sensitivity analysis.
•	Outliers at the bin level (±3 SD within participant) will be excluded prior to aggregation.
•	Participants with unusable full-condition recordings will be excluded before analysis.
•	Random-effects structure will be simplified if convergence fails or singular fit occurs.
________________________________________
9. Reporting
For each DV we will report:
•	Fixed effect estimates
•	Planned contrasts (corrected p-values)
•	Effect sizes (standardized beta or marginal R²)
•	Estimated marginal means with 95% confidence intervals
•	Convergence diagnostics
Primary confirmatory inferences will be based on Model 1 (difference-score model with Static as reference).
All other analyses are confirmatory extensions or exploratory as specified above.
table.transformations:
Coding of Categorical Variables
Condition (4 levels: Static, Speeding, Slowing, Adaptive Delayed)
Primary confirmatory models will use treatment (dummy) coding with Static as the reference level.
Under this scheme:
•	The intercept represents the mean of the Static condition.
•	Coefficients for Speeding, Slowing, and Adaptive represent deviations from Static.
As a sensitivity analysis, models will also be refit using sum-contrast coding, where:
•	The intercept represents the grand mean across conditions.
•	Each condition coefficient represents deviation from the grand mean.
Segment (Baseline vs Stimulation)
Dummy coded with Baseline as reference in models comparing segments.
________________________________________
Continuous Predictors
All continuous moderators and covariates (e.g., MAIA-2, MISS, ITQ, baseline respiration rate) will be mean-centered prior to analysis.
Time variables in growth models:
•	TimeWithinSegment (0–7 bins) will be centered.
•	Time2 (quadratic term) will be computed after centering Time.
•	For models including both baseline and stimulation, TimeWithinSegment will reset within each segment (0–7 per segment).
________________________________________
Difference Scores
For primary analyses, change scores will be computed as:
Delta_DV = mean(DV_stimulation) − mean(DV_baseline)
These difference scores will be used directly in LMMs without further centering unless included in interaction models.
________________________________________
Physiological Transformations
•	LF and HF HRV spectral power will be log-transformed if distributions are positively skewed.
•	If additional variables exhibit strong skewness or heteroscedasticity, appropriate transformations (e.g., log) will be applied consistently across all conditions before modeling.
•	No rank-based or nonparametric transformations are planned unless model assumptions are severely violated.
________________________________________
Standardization
Continuous predictors used in moderation analyses may additionally be z-standardized (mean = 0, SD = 1) for interpretability of interaction terms; this will not affect significance tests.
table.inference_criteria:
All primary analyses will be conducted within a frequentist framework.
________________________________________
Significance Threshold
•	Statistical significance will be evaluated using two-tailed tests.
•	Alpha level: p < .05.
Fixed effects in linear mixed-effects models will be evaluated using the Satterthwaite approximation for denominator degrees of freedom.
________________________________________
Model Evaluation
For each model, we will report:
•	Fixed effect estimates (beta coefficients)
•	Standard errors
•	t-values
•	p-values
•	95% confidence intervals
•	Marginal R² (variance explained by fixed effects)
•	Conditional R² (variance explained by fixed + random effects)
Omnibus effects of Condition will be evaluated using:
•	Wald tests from the LMM output, and/or
•	Likelihood-ratio tests comparing nested models (with vs without Condition).
________________________________________
Planned Comparisons
For the primary confirmatory difference-score models:
•	Planned contrasts comparing Speeding, Slowing, and Adaptive to Static
•	Additional contrast: Adaptive vs Slowing, Adaptive vs Speeding, Speeding vs Slowing
Multiple comparisons within each dependent variable will be corrected using Holm correction.
________________________________________
Multiple Dependent Variables
Primary confirmatory outcomes are:
•	Respiration rate
•	Auditory–respiratory MPC
•	RSA / HF-HRV
•	ETCO₂
•	EMG
•	SRSI
•	Nijmegen score
Holm correction will be applied within each DV for condition contrasts.
Across DVs, results will be interpreted with consideration of consistency of pattern rather than strict familywise correction across all physiological systems.
Exploratory correlation analyses will use False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction across all tested correlations.
________________________________________
Moderation Analyses
Condition × Moderator interaction effects will be evaluated at p < .05.
Holm correction will be applied across moderation tests within each DV.
Significant interactions will be followed by simple slopes tests at:
•	−1 SD
•	Mean
•	+1 SD
________________________________________
Model Assumptions
Residual normality and homoscedasticity will be assessed using:
•	Q–Q plots
•	Residual vs fitted plots
If assumptions are substantially violated:
•	Log transformation (e.g., HRV spectral power) will be applied.
•	Robust standard errors will be reported as a sensitivity analysis.
________________________________________
Convergence Criteria
If a maximal random-effects model fails to converge or yields a singular fit:
1.	Random slopes will be removed.
2.	The simplified model will be used for inference.
All model simplifications will be documented.
________________________________________
Interpretation
Primary confirmatory inferences will be based on the difference-score models with Static as reference.
Growth-curve models, baseline-covariate models, correlation matrices, and moderation analyses will be interpreted as confirmatory extensions (if preregistered) or exploratory, as specified above.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Participant-level inclusion
A participant dataset will be included if the participant:
•	Meets all inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria at screening,
•	Completes the full laboratory session (all four conditions),
•	Provides usable physiological recordings for the primary signals needed for analysis (at minimum: respiration; and for cardiac outcomes: ECG).
Participant-level exclusion
A participant will be excluded from all confirmatory analyses if any of the following apply:
•	Withdrawal of consent or incomplete session (did not complete all four conditions),
•	Protocol violation that meaningfully compromises interpretation (e.g., removing sensors for a substantial portion of the task; repeated talking/movement despite reminders; failure to follow safety instructions),
•	Missing or unusable respiration signal for one or more full conditions (because respiration is required for the primary entrainment outcomes and for computing bin-level and baseline–stimulation difference scores),
•	For ECG-based outcomes specifically: unusable ECG signal for one or more full conditions (participants may still be retained for respiration-only outcomes if respiration is usable).
Participants who are found post hoc to meet an exclusion criterion (e.g., undisclosed relevant diagnosis, pregnancy) will be removed.
Segment/bin-level exclusion (within included participants)
Data will be excluded at the bin or breath/beat level (rather than excluding the entire participant) when artifacts are localized:
•	30-second bins with clear sensor dropouts, clipping, or gross motion artifacts will be marked invalid and excluded from bin-level analyses.
•	Respiration (breath-level): breaths with failed detection (e.g., incomplete cycles) will be excluded from breath-derived metrics (RR, IER, breath duration variability).
•	ECG (beat-level): ectopic beats and detection errors will be corrected using standard artifact correction; segments with excessive R-peak detection failure will be excluded.
•	ETCO₂ (breath-level): breaths without a reliable expiratory plateau (or otherwise invalid end-tidal estimate) will be excluded from ETCO₂ averaging.
If, after bin/breath/beat exclusions, a condition has insufficient valid data to compute reliable segment means (e.g., fewer than 4 valid 30-second bins in baseline or stimulation), that condition will be treated as missing for that DV for that participant.
Outliers
Outlier handling will be applied at two levels:
1.	Bin-level outliers (primary approach): within each participant and DV, 30-second bins with values > ±3 SD from that participant’s mean (for that DV within that condition/segment) will be flagged as outliers and excluded for bin-level analyses.
2.	Aggregated outcomes (sensitivity approach): if condition-level Delta scores (stimulation − baseline) contain extreme values, analyses will be repeated with and without those observations to assess robustness. Both results will be reported if conclusions differ.
Missing data
•	Mixed-effects models will use all available valid observations (i.e., they can accommodate some missing bins/conditions).
•	Participants will not be excluded solely due to a small number of missing bins, provided segment-level summaries remain computable.
•	Participant-level exclusions will be limited to cases where primary signals are unusable for a full condition or the session is incomplete.
All exclusions (participant-level and bin/breath/beat-level) will be documented, including counts and reasons.
table.missing_data_handling:
Analyses will be conducted on all available valid data. Linear mixed-effects models will use all non-missing observations (bins/segments) without imputing missing values, under the assumption that missingness is primarily due to technical artifacts (e.g., transient sensor dropouts) rather than the experimental manipulation.
No imputation is planned for physiological or questionnaire outcomes.
Handling rules:
•	Bin-level missingness: Invalid 30-second bins (artifact/dropout) will be excluded; remaining bins will be used. Mixed models will naturally accommodate unequal numbers of bins.
•	Breath/beat-level missingness: Invalid breaths (respiration/ETCO₂) and invalid beats (ECG) will be excluded during preprocessing; segment/bin summaries will be computed from the remaining valid samples.
•	Condition-level missingness: If a participant has insufficient valid data to compute a baseline or stimulation mean for a given condition and DV (e.g., fewer than 4 valid 30-second bins in baseline or stimulation), that condition will be treated as missing for that DV for that participant.
•	Participant-level missingness: Participants with unusable respiration data for an entire condition will be excluded from confirmatory analyses requiring respiration-derived measures; participants may still be retained for other outcomes if those signals are usable and the session is complete.
The amount and pattern of missing data (by signal, condition, and segment) will be reported, along with reasons (e.g., sensor dropout, plateau detection failure for ETCO₂).

text.text: Auditory feedback may influence breathing without explicit instructions to regulate it, but its precise impact remains unclear.
We examined responses to adaptive and nonadaptive breath-like sounds during passive listening.

Thirty-nine young adults completed four counterbalanced conditions: nonrhythmic filtered noise (Static), rhythmic sounds progressively slowing or speeding relative to initial breathing rate (Slowing and Speeding respectively), and sound adapting continuously to respiratory frequency and phase with a prescribed phase delay relative to respiration (Adaptive).
Each condition included 4 min of nominal silence followed by 4 min of stimulation.
Primary outcomes were breathing rate slopes, auditory-respiratory phase locking as a measure of auditory-respiratory coordination, respiratory sinus arrhythmia, and subjective relaxation.
Breathing-rate trajectories differed across conditions; Adaptive showed a more negative slope than Static, although average rates were similar.
Phase locking was higher and more sustained during Adaptive than during the nonadaptive rhythmic conditions.
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia trajectories differed, but planned contrasts did not survive multiplicity correction.
A relaxation composite score did not differ by condition, but an item-level analysis indicated less physical relaxation after Adaptive than Static.
Secondary outcomes provided no evidence of increased cardiorespiratory coupling or reduced upper-trapezius muscle activity.

Interestingly, the negative breathing-rate trajectories remained significantly different in Adaptive compared to Static after retaining only the 25 respondents that did not notice the sound's adaptation to their breathing.
These findings support adaptive auditory stimulation as a means of supporting auditory-respiratory coordination during uninstructed listening, with a modest and relative change in breathing rate.
Clinical benefits and independence from intentional breathing control remain to be tested.
Breathing is an accessible target for psychophysiological self-regulation because it is generated automatically while remaining sensitive to voluntary control and sensory context.
Slow breathing and heart-rate-variability (HRV) biofeedback leverage this flexibility to modify cardiorespiratory activity.

In resonance-frequency biofeedback, breathing near an individually determined frequency, typically approximately six breaths per minute, amplifies cardiovascular oscillations through interactions between respiratory and baroreflex processes (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014).
text.formatted: In resonance-frequency biofeedback, breathing near an individually determined frequency, typically approximately six breaths per minute, amplifies cardiovascular oscillations through interactions between respiratory and baroreflex processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Breathing interventions can also reduce self-reported stress and anxiety, although a meta-analysis of randomized trials identified methodological limitations and variation across studies that constrain general conclusions (Fincham et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Breathing interventions can also reduce self-reported stress and anxiety, although a meta-analysis of randomized trials identified methodological limitations and variation across studies that constrain general conclusions <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Fincham et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For applied psychophysiology, the challenge is to establish which forms of respiratory guidance change breathing, which changes accompany subjective benefit, and under what conditions those benefits occur.
Slow paced breathing is not equivalent to relaxation.
The resulting breathing pattern and the effort involved may both shape the experience.

Previous work suggests that relaxation can vary with the inhalation-to-exhalation ratio (Van Diest et al., 2014), while following a prescribed rhythm can lead to hyperventilation in untrained subjects (Szulczewski, 2019) and require effort, particularly when it differs from spontaneous breathing (Fincham et al., 2023; Gholamrezaei et al., 2021; Stark et al., 2000).

text.text: Breathing instructions may also influence attention and expectations alongside respiratory changes (Vlemincx & Cortez-Vázquez, 2024).
text.formatted: Breathing instructions may also influence attention and expectations alongside respiratory changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Vlemincx & Cortez-Vázquez, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This makes it worthwhile to explore guidance that supports respiratory adjustment without requiring continuous deliberate control.
Sound provides a possible route to such guidance without imposing additional task demands.

Musical rhythms can influence respiratory timing, with earlier work documenting changes in breath-period variability and in the relationships between breathing and perceived rhythm (Bernardi et al., 2017; Haas et al., 1986; Mollakazemi et al., 2019).

text.text: The auditory signal also matters: previous research has shown how ecological breathing sounds reduce breath-duration variability more than artificial sounds with comparable temporal features (Murgia et al., 2016).

text.text: These observations suggest that sound can provide temporal information relevant to respiratory timing.
Sonification extends this approach by making sound contingent on physiological activity.
In an earlier study, we developed tempo-and phase-aligned breathing sonification using participants' keyboard indications of inhalation and exhalation (Van Kerrebroeck & Maes, 2021).

text.text: That procedure demonstrated a practical route to respiratory feedback, but reporting each breath using keyboard presses necessarily engaged participants with their breathing.

Evidence for respiratory modulation without deliberate synchronization comes from Janson et al. (2013), who presented delayed versions of participants' breathing signals as auditory and visual feedback.

text.text: Participants were instructed to breathe comfortably without consciously adapting to the signals; moderate delays slowed breathing in 11 of 24 participants, although responses varied and feedback induced irregular breathing in some individuals (Janson et al., 2013).

text.text: In a complementary approach, (Leslie et al., 2019) presented ambient music with fixed, personalized, or continuously respiratory-driven amplitude modulation while participants performed an attention-demanding task.

text.text: Breathing slowed across the music conditions, with the strongest effect for a tempo set below the individual's baseline rate.
Together, these studies motivate to investigate the potential of personalized sound with continuous physiological sensing for respiratory regulation without an instruction to synchronize.
Building on this work, a central question is whether continuous adaptation offers an advantage over a personalized auditory rhythm that changes independently of breathing.
An open-loop rhythm may begin near a person's spontaneous breathing rate but become increasingly mismatched as its tempo changes.
Continuous adaptation could preserve a temporal relationship as breathing fluctuates, while an added phase offset may encourage gradual changes in respiratory timing.
This creates the possibility of guiding breathing through sustained coordination with sound.

Evaluating this possibility requires examining both auditory-respiratory phase locking and changes in breathing rate: phase locking captures the coordination maintained by the feedback, while changes in breathing rate indicate whether participants' respiration also adjusts during exposure.

The present experiment compared four auditory conditions during passive listening: nonrhythmic filtered noise (Static), breath-like sounds that progressively slowed or accelerated relative to initial breathing rate (Slowing and Speeding), and a breath-like sound that continuously adapted to respiratory frequency and phase with a configured phase delay (Adaptive).
Participants received no instruction to regulate their breathing.
Four preregistered hypotheses on primary outcomes addressed auditory-respiratory coordination and relaxation.

Relative to Static, Slowing and Adaptive were expected to produce lower breathing rates slopes (H1), greater respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA; H3), and greater subjective relaxation (H4), with the opposite pattern expected during Speeding.
Auditory-respiratory phase locking values (PLVs) were expected to be larger in Adaptive than Slowing, and larger during Slowing than Speeding (H2).
Hypotheses on secondary outcomes predicted stronger cardiorespiratory phase locking during Slowing and Adaptive than Speeding (S1).

They also predicted higher relative CO₂ levels (S2), lower uppertrapezius muscle activity (S3), and a lower hyperventilation composite score (S4) during Slowing and Adaptive than Static, with the opposite pattern during Speeding.
Together, these analyses examined how adaptive auditory stimulation shapes auditory-respiratory coordination and whether this is accompanied by physiological and subjective relaxation.
Forty-two adults were recruited through the university's experiment-participation platform and tested in the Health Psychology laboratory at KU Leuven.
Three participants with cold-related obstructed breathing or excessive movement were excluded before statistical analysis.
The final sample comprised 39 participants, aged 18-21 years (M = 18.59, SD = 0.88). 34 reported female and five male sex assigned at birth.
All completed the four conditions.
Six participants reported formal musical training (M = 6.0, SD = 2.37).

Among the 39 participants, 15 performed physical exercise or sports 1-2 times per week, 13 exercised 3-4 times per week, four exercised at least five times per week, six never exercised, and one preferred not to say.

The recruitment target of 40 allowed for 10% attrition and was based on a G*Power analysis for a four-condition within-participant design, assuming Cohen's f = .25, α = .05, and 80% power, informed by Van Diest et al. (2014).

text.text: Eligibility required age 18-35 years and comprehension of written and spoken English.

Exclusion criteria were recent psychotropic-medication use; cardiac or respiratory disorders, hearing impairment, or psychiatric disorders within the preceding two years; pregnancy; and breathing-exercise or mindfulness practice at least twice weekly during the preceding month.
Participants avoided strenuous exercise and alcohol for at least 12 h before testing.
They provided written informed consent and received course credits.
The KU Leuven ethics committee approved the study (G-2025-10319).

text.text: The within-participant design comprised Static, Slowing, Speeding, and Adaptive conditions, each presented once.
Condition order was counterbalanced across participants using all 24 possible sequences.
Each sequence was used once or twice across the 39 participants analyzed.
Each condition comprised 4 min of nominal silence followed by 4 min of auditory stimulation.
The study was preregistered at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/GCVQE.

text.text: Primary outcomes were breathing rate slopes, auditory-respiratory PLV, RSA, and subjective relaxation.
Secondary outcomes were cardiorespiratory PLV, % change in end-expiratory carbon dioxide levels, upper-trapezius muscle activity, and Nijmegen Questionnaire symptoms.
Procedure Participants first completed demographic, baseline-state, and individual-difference questionnaires, followed by sensor attachment and signal checks (approximately 20 min).
A 4-min familiarization with constant-tempo sound also included three approximately 5-s arm elevations, separated by approximately 10 s, to provide a functional EMG reference.
Experimental EMG amplitudes were normalized to this recording (see Online Resource for further details).
During the experimental trials, participants were instructed to sit quietly, remain still, and listen to the played back sounds.
They could keep their eyes open or closed and received no instruction to regulate or synchronize their breathing.
Each trial was followed by experience ratings (approximately 5 min) and a short break (approximately 2 min).
Final questionnaires and debriefing followed the four trials.
The visit duration was approximately 90 min.
The stimulus was synthesized in Pure Data from filtered pink noise, with amplitude and spectral modulation producing a breath-like sound.
It was delivered through Sennheiser HD 620S headphones at a reported level of 50 dB.
Participants confirmed comfortable, low-to-medium loudness during familiarization.
Static used the filtered noise without a rhythmic amplitude or filtered frequency envelope (see Online Resource for further details).

Slowing and Speeding used the amplitude and spectral modulated sound that began at an estimate of the participant's spontaneous respiratory frequency at the end of the silent period and progressed linearly toward 80% and 120% of that initial frequency, respectively, over 4 min of the stimulation period.
A 5-s audio gain ramp began at approximately 235 s, with full dynamic control beginning at 240 s.
Online frequency estimates used a rolling 10-s respiratory window and were updated every 0.5 s.
Adaptive used ongoing respiratory frequency and phase to control an auditory oscillator.
The controller combined the rolling frequency estimate with a sinusoidal phase-error correction and a configured phase offset of -0.10 cycles (-36°), selected through pilot testing.
This offset was intended to encourage slower breathing by positioning the auditory rhythm slightly behind the respiratory cycle.
Respiratory activity continuously influenced the sound, and any participant response could alter the signal subsequently driving the controller.
The audio waveform and audio phase was recorded alongside the physiological signals.
Online estimation, signal processing, and controller details are provided in Online Resource, Section S1.
Physiological signals were acquired with a BIOPAC MP160 at 2,000 Hz.
A Vernier respiration belt connected to a gas-pressure sensor and positioned at the lower rib cage of participants recorded respiratory movements around the torso.
Breathing rate and phase refer to quantities derived from these movements.
Electrocardiography used a Vernier ECG Sensor with right-clavicle and left-lower rib electrode positions and a right-lower rib reference.

Bipolar upper-trapezius electromyography (EMG) used pre-gelled Ag/AgCl electrodes aligned with the muscle fibres near the midpoint between C7 and the acromion, approximately 20 mm apart, with a reference over C7.
An Arduino interface supplied the respiratory signal for online auditory control.
Synchronization pulses linked its logs to BIOPAC recordings.
Expired carbon dioxide was sampled continuously through a nasal cannula using a Vacumed 17515A capnograph.
End-expiratory plateau values were summarized in 30-second bins and expressed as percentage change relative to the mean voltage during the final 2 min of the corresponding silence period.
See the Online Resource for additional details.
The primary subjective outcome was a composite score as the mean of three 1-7 ratings selected from the Smith Relaxation States Inventory (Smith, 2001): At Ease, Distant, and Physically Relaxed.
Three additional items assessed stress-related experiences: Troublesome Thoughts, Discomfort, and Tight and Tense.
The composite score was the primary measure of subjective relaxation; separate analyses of all six individual items were exploratory.

The secondary symptom outcome summed six selected Nijmegen Questionnaire items: Heart Racing, Short of Breath, Dizzy Spells, Fingers Tingling, Unable to Breathe Deeply, and Tight Chest (Van Dixhoorn & Duivenvoorden, 1985).

text.text: These items were selected to assess bodily symptoms relevant to the breathing manipulation while limiting the burden of repeated postcondition assessment.
The resulting score was treated as a study-specific symptom index.

Exploratory post-condition ratings assessed pleasure, arousal, and dominance (i.e. perceived control) of the sounds with the Self-Assessment Manikin (Bradley & Lang, 1994), and estimated time spent with closed eyes, mind wandering, attending to breathing, controlling breathing, or feeling sleepy.

text.text: Breathing cycles were detected as trough-peak-trough sequences after lowpass filtering at 2 Hz and resampling to 100 Hz.
Cycle duration was defined as the interval between consecutive troughs, and breathing rate was calculated as 60 divided by cycle duration in seconds.
Cyclespecific rates were then averaged within each 30-s window.
Respiratory phase was derived from the analytic signal of the filtered trace and aligned with logged auditory phase.
Auditory-respiratory PLV was the magnitude of the mean unit vector of their phase differences, calculated within 30-s bins (Lachaux et al., 1999).

text.text: PLV ranges from 0 (phase differences dispersed across the analysis interval) to 1 (a constant phase difference).
Static had no defined auditory phase and was excluded from PLV analyses.
ECG processing identified R peaks, rejected implausible or locally discrepant intervals, and interpolated invalid intervals.
ECG-derived normal-to-normal (NN) intervals underwent artifact screening and correction before HRV computation (Laborde et al., 2017).

Physiological preprocessing used Python 3.14.2; statistical analyses used R 4.5.2.
Detailed processing parameters, exploratory measures, and the analysis mapping are provided in Online Resource, Sections S1-S3.
The analysis distinguished hypotheses concerning primary outcomes (H1-H4), hypotheses concerning secondary outcomes (S1-S4), and exploratory analyses.
Time-course 30s-bin models included condition, centered bin time, and their interaction, with an AR(1) residual structure within participant-condition series.
Time was coded 0-7 and centered at 3.5.
Condition-level contrasts compared model-estimated values at mid-stimulation, equal to the average across the eight bin positions.
Slope contrasts compared rates of change per 30-s bin.
Static was the reference except for auditory-respiratory PLV, for which Slowing was the reference.
The planned random structure included participant intercepts and time slopes and participant-condition intercepts.
Normalized EMG used participant intercepts only due to a singular model fit.

Omnibus tests used marginal Wald F-tests and containment degrees of freedom of the nlme library in R. Estimated means and trends used the emmeans library in R. Adding quadratic time did not improve fit for any of the repeated-bin outcomes (likelihood-ratio p ≥ .154), so linear trajectories are reported.
Confirmatory participant-level slope ANOVAs are reported in Online Resource.
Post-condition ratings and full-stimulation physiological summaries were analyzed with condition as a fixed effect and participant intercepts.
Self-report models used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.
Condition contrasts were Holm-adjusted separately within outcome and model.
Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied to specified exploratory families.
Unadjusted, Holm-adjusted, and Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted values are denoted p, pHolm, and pFDR, respectively.
Confidence intervals are nominal 95% intervals.

text.text: Breath awareness, breath control, pleasure, arousal, sleepiness, eyes closed, and mind wandering showed no corrected condition effects.
Of the 38 respondents, 25 (65.8%) reported not noticing that sound adapted to their breathing.
Among those who answered "No," Adaptive retained higher auditory-respiratory PLV than Slowing and Speeding, and its breathing-rate slope was more negative than Static (pHolm = .043).
Further exploratory analyses, including individual differences, respiratory variability, and HRV, are presented in Online Resource, Section S6.
Adaptive breath-like sound sustained auditory-respiratory coordination during passive listening and was associated with a relative slowing of breathing compared with nonrhythmic sound.
This change in breathing-rate was also present among participants who reported not having noticed that the sound adapted to their breathing.

Participants also reported lower physical relaxation in the adaptive condition, raising the possibility that auditory guidance drew breathing away from a comfortable and spontaneous pattern established during the silent baseline.
Alternatively, the more irregular auditory rhythm produced by continuous adaptation may have been less calming.
Together, these findings suggest that adaptive sound can support respiratory adjustment without explicit recognition of the feedback or an immediate increase in relaxation.
This distinction provides a basis for exploring when such guidance could benefit relaxation training and self-regulation.
Continuous adaptation sustained auditory-respiratory coordination over time.
Participants maintained stable phase locking in the Adaptive condition, whereas phase locking declined during both the Slowing and Speeding conditions.
These open-loop rhythms began near each participant's spontaneous breathing rate but progressively moved away from it.
Continuous adaptation may thus help preserve an effective temporal relationship by accommodating fluctuations in breathing as they occur.
A progressively slowing or speeding and non-adaptive rhythm, in contrast, may become increasingly difficult to follow once its timing diverges from ongoing respiration.

This provides a plausible explanation for why prescribing a slower auditory trajectory alone did not produce the expected respiratory response, while an adaptive stimulus sustained coupling and was associated with relative slowing.
Adaptive stimulation was associated with a change in breathing behavior.

The Adaptive-Static slope difference corresponded to approximately 1.27 breaths/min of relative divergence across stimulation, comprising an estimated decrease of 0.62 breaths/min in Adaptive and an increase of 0.66 breaths/min in Static.
This contrast remained significant after adjustment for pre-stimulation breathing rate, suggesting that differences in initial breathing rate did not fully account for the observed divergence.
As such, the combined pattern of stable phase locking and respiratory slowing supports entrainment as a plausible interpretation.
A dynamical systems account offers a possible explanation of this pattern.
In oscillator models, synchronization depends on the mismatch between interacting rhythms, their coupling, and the tendency to return toward a preferred rate (Savinov et al., 2021).

text.text: Models of auditory-motor synchronization further show how adaptation to external timing can coexist with a persistent attraction toward an individual's spontaneous tempo (Roman et al., 2023).

text.text: Applied to respiration, this suggests that continuous tracking could keep the auditory rhythm within an effective synchronization range as breathing fluctuates.

Within this maintained interaction, the configured phase offset might encourage small, repeated delays in respiratory timing that accumulate into longer breath cycles, similar to findings using delayed auditory and visual feedback of participants' own breathing (Janson et al., 2013).

text.text: This mechanism would account for the combination of sustained phase locking and relative slowing in Adaptive, whereas a progressively diverging nonadaptive rhythm may eventually lose its influence.
Adaptation may therefore support a gradual respiratory slowing by maintaining auditory-respiratory coordination with a phase offset intended to keep the auditory rhythm slightly behind breathing.
A further prediction is that adaptation could enlarge the basin of attraction, allowing coordination to emerge from a wider set of initial states.
Systematically varying initial phase, frequency mismatch, controller strength, and phase offset would help establish when coordination develops and whether it produces respiratory slowing.
The findings extend evidence that auditory timing can shape respiration (Bernardi et al., 2017; Haas et al., 1986).

(Leslie et al., 2019) similarly demonstrated respiratory slowing with personalized musical modulation while participants performed another task.

text.text: Together, these approaches indicate that individualized auditory timing can influence breathing across different attentional settings.

The present study adds evidence that real-time adaptation can sustain the temporal relationship throughout exposure, providing a practical foundation for respiratory guidance without an explicit synchronization task.
Respiratory coordination and perceived relaxation followed different patterns.
Adaptive sustained auditory-respiratory coordination and produced relative respiratory slowing but received lower Physically Relaxed ratings than Static.
Exploratory ratings also indicated lower perceived control during Adaptive and Slowing.
Several factors could explain this pattern.
The modest respiratory slowing, with rates remaining near 16 breaths/min, may have been insufficient to produce a detectable relaxation benefit during four minutes of stimulation.
Meanwhile, the more irregular auditory rhythm generated by continuous adaptation may have been less predictable and less calming.
Lower perceived control also suggests that the experience of being guided deserves consideration alongside the physiological response.

The experience of respiratory guidance may depend on both its demands and its psychological context. (Stark et al., 2000) found that participants reported greater effort and lower accuracy when the prescribed breathing frequency deviated further from their spontaneous rate.

text.text: Although their study involved deliberate pacing, it suggests that adjusting breathing to an external rhythm can impose demands that may offset relaxation benefits.
Expectations may also contribute: experimentally enhancing expectations increased the subjective benefits of deep breathing (Szabo & Kocsis, 2017).
text.formatted: Expectations may also contribute: experimentally enhancing expectations increased the subjective benefits of deep breathing <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Szabo & Kocsis, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, (Fincham et al., 2023) found no additional psychological benefit of breathing at approximately 5.5 rather than 12 breaths/min under matched guidance, suggesting that breathing rate alone does not determine subjective outcomes.

text.text: Here, participants listened without instructions to regulate their breathing, providing a different context from deliberate relaxation exercises.

Future studies could vary auditory predictability and explicit breathing instructions while assessing effort, expectations, and perceived control to establish when respiratory guidance also promotes relaxation.
Respiratory adaptation may also occur without explicit recognition of the feedback.
Of 38 respondents, 25 reported not noticing that the sound adapted to their breathing.
In this subgroup, Adaptive retained higher phase locking than both nonadaptive rhythmic conditions and a more negative breathing-rate slope than Static.

Recent research similarly suggests that respiratory timing can align with auditory rhythms without explicit instructions to synchronize breathing. (Andrews et al., 2025) observed mild auditory-respiratory entrainment during a rhythmic attention task, while (Muñoz-Caracuel et al., 2024) found respiratory entrainment during active auditory discrimination, although not during passive exposure.

text.text: The present findings add evidence from passive listening, with respiratory adjustment also observed among participants who did not recognize the adaptive contingency.
Together, these observations support the possibility that auditory guidance can influence respiratory timing without listeners explicitly recognizing how the sound responds to their breathing.
For biofeedback, these findings suggest that acquiring a new respiratory pattern and finding it comfortable may unfold on different timescales.

In a study of instructed breathing at six breaths/min, (Szulczewski, 2019) found improved CO₂ regulation with practice and increases in calmness and relaxation at later assessments, but not the initial session.
text.formatted: In a study of instructed breathing at six breaths/min, <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Szulczewski, 2019)</ref> found improved CO₂ regulation with practice and increases in calmness and relaxation at later assessments, but not the initial session.

text.text: Although that task involved substantially slower and explicitly paced breathing, it demonstrates that immediate experience need not predict the experience after familiarization.

Repeated exposure, gentler timing adjustments, and opportunities for the listener to influence the degree of guidance are therefore promising ways to test whether sustained coordination can become both effective and comfortable.
The silent baseline provides a basis for exploring how responses to adaptive sound may depend on the listener's initial physiological state.
A respiratory influence was detectable after several minutes of quiet sitting, without first inducing stress or asking participants to change their breathing.
A next step could be to test adaptive guidance during recovery from an experimentally elevated respiratory state.
If a listener is breathing faster than their usual resting pattern, an individually tuned slowing influence may facilitate a return toward that pattern and be experienced more positively.
Comparing rest and stress-recovery conditions would directly test this possibility while measuring both respiratory change and subjectively felt recovery.
The aim would be to identify when and for whom a given degree of guidance is helpful, building on proposals to personalize breathing interventions (Vlemincx & Cortez-Vázquez, 2024).
text.formatted: The aim would be to identify when and for whom a given degree of guidance is helpful, building on proposals to personalize breathing interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Vlemincx & Cortez-Vázquez, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Another application could be to build on the continuous adaptation principle for respiratory support during recovery from critical illness, including weaning from mechanical ventilation.

Music already has a clinical precedent in this setting: patient-directed listening reduced anxiety relative to usual care and reduced some measures of sedative exposure in mechanically ventilated patients (Chlan et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Music already has a clinical precedent in this setting: patient-directed listening reduced anxiety relative to usual care and reduced some measures of sedative exposure in mechanically ventilated patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Chlan et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Adaptive respiratory guidance could be investigated as a support for responsive patients during the transition to independent breathing.
In such a setting, the objective would be comfortable, physiologically appropriate breathing, with targets determined by respiratory demand and clinical assessment rather than by slowing alone.
The sample was young, predominantly female, and nonclinical, and participants experienced each condition only once, for 4 min.
Further research should therefore examine broader populations, repeated exposure, and the potential for lasting improvements in self-regulation.
Future evaluations should distinguish changes in breathing from benefits to the individual.
Matched replay conditions and separate manipulations of controller components could clarify the role of adaptive feedback and the direction of influence between sound and breathing.

Longer recordings and calibrated capnography would strengthen physiological interpretation, while measures of comfort, perceived agency, and intentional breathing control could establish how sustained coordination shapes the listening experience.

The present findings support adaptive auditory stimulation as a promising approach to respiratory coordination without explicit synchronization instructions and provide a basis for evaluating its potential in clinical and self-regulation settings.

Adaptive breath-like sound sustained auditory-respiratory coordination and shifted breathing-rate trajectories toward relative slowing during uninstructed listening, including among participants who did not report recognizing the adaptive contingency.
The combination supports spontaneous entrainment as a facilitatory account of the interaction.

Its coexistence with lower physical relaxation makes the findings informative about how respiratory guidance is experienced, suggesting that adjustment of breathing and immediate subjective benefit depend on different aspects of the interaction.

Continuous adaptation thus provides a basis for studying how sound can guide spontaneous respiration, and for developing personalized biofeedback that matches the listener's physiological state, comfort, and therapeutic goals.
